tags.gist: Draws a lesson from a missed docket: an AI can do exactly what it is asked and still fail because the human asked wrongly.
A nurse and patient advocate strongly supports responsible AI, seeing potential to widen access to current knowledge, improve consistency and spot risk sooner.
Argues AI must learn to notice when the request differs from the need, since people ask proxy questions, minimize symptoms and omit what matters.
Worries that patient-facing and agentic tools that look administrative can shape care, and says a regulatory boundary must not become a safety gap.
Calls the framework a useful start but says incorrect output does not cover the full range of foreseeable patient harm.
Illustrates with a diabetic patient who asks only for his insurance card while having a heart attack: the AI answered correctly and he died.
Says patients ask administrative questions about cost, podiatrists or rescheduling when the real need is clinical, which the framework should recognize.
Wants risk to also cover incomplete interactions, missed latent need, omission, false reassurance, care delay from cost information, follow-up duty and cumulative turns.
Cites a patient-agent benchmark showing agents fulfilled administrative requests without clinically screening patients, as empirical support for widening the framework.
Says completing the task is no measure of safety; patient-facing systems should be tested on spotting when a request is a proxy for a need.
Agrees the categories blur: cost estimates, coverage explanations and urgency assessments direct action without imperative wording, so foreseeable influence should count.
Proposes that oversight track a technology's degree of influence on whether, when, where and from whom care happens, including administrative and benefits tools.
Wants personalization, conversational authority, repeated prompting and selective presentation of options weighed as ways to shape choice without a command.
Agrees patient-facing risk differs but warns licensure does not make clinicians reliable safeguards, since no practitioner can stay current with all evidence.
Sees AI's promise in anchoring clinicians to current evidence against habit and overconfidence, rather than reproducing existing practice variation.
Wants both AI and practitioner judged against a current evidence-based standard, urging a common nationally recognized clinical reference framework.
Says common is not appropriate and cites mature guideline systems to argue AI should operationalize curated evidence, not derive a standard from training data.
Says the safest model is neither AI instead of clinicians nor clinicians as an unquestioned backstop, but AI plus clinician plus an updated evidence standard.
Wants whole encounters evaluated with scenarios where the key clinical fact is absent from the first request, scoring whether the AI knew to ask more.
Frames triage risk as probability times severity times consequence of delay, asking whether AI weighs rare catastrophic possibilities against needless escalation.
Wants triage and level-of-care functions shown to be grounded in curated evidence-based sources with provenance, not improvised from the internet.
Accepts the approach if competency spans knowledge, reasoning, recognition of danger and restraint about acting independently.
Wants a specific competency added for recognizing latent clinical need inside apparently administrative interactions.
Wants administrative-intent versus clinical-need recognition tested, with task completion and safety scored separately so completion cannot offset missed triage.
Wants competency tests to check whether the AI recognizes when a simple request warrants more questions before closing the encounter.
Says benchmarks need messy humans who minimize, omit and ask proxy questions, and should test premature closure after apparent success.
Cautions against making the average clinician the final standard, preferring a comparator that includes a current evidence-based clinical standard.
Describes how AI could keep current evidence alongside human judgment to counter anchoring, outdated training and overconfidence.
Wants evaluation against three comparators: the best evidence-based standard, current unaided practice, and the human-AI team.
Supports comparing with care absent the device but wants an evidence-based ideal alongside, separating better-than-today from acceptably safe.
Backs third parties for high-impact systems, with substantive independence, conflict disclosure and safeguards against cherry-picking and barriers to competition.
Accepts the trade only within limits, with tolerance shrinking as harm, irreversibility, autonomy, patient contact and vulnerability rise.
Wants monitoring to follow the chain from output through decision, care, claim and outcome, since technical metrics alone are not enough.
Wants outcomes that matter clinically and near misses tracked, such as delayed care, abandonment after cost information, overrides and wrong routing.
Wants accessible channels for clinicians, patients and caregivers to report suspected AI problems into an auditable safety-learning system.
Accepts supervisory AI for anomaly, drift and tool-use detection but not as final judge; it must be validated, auditable and under human governance.
Insists responsibility that is shared must still be owned, with each party accountable for its part and patients never made to find failures.
Wants consequential interactions reconstructable: what was said, what the AI knew, which version answered, what evidence and warnings applied.
Says contracts can allocate tasks but not accountability, so no link in the long healthcare AI chain can disclaim its part after harm.
Says deployers cannot disclaim provider-made model changes and wants notification, versioning, regression testing, revalidation, rollback and contingency plans.
Says agents act, so the question becomes whether the whole chain was appropriate, since individually correct steps can add up to abandoned care.
Names a clinical-adjacent safety gap and asks who regulates influential non-device AI, urging coordinated oversight proportionate to influence.
Points to coverage-algorithm litigation and state laws as safety signals and wants a structured FDA mechanism to monitor such external developments.
Wants AI to move knowledge rather than patients, judged on evidence grounding, recognizing generalist limits and escalating when specialists are needed.
Wants evidence to rise with foreseeable clinical influence, with the risk framework also counting omission, delay, autonomy and lack of human review.
Wants stronger real-world and prospective human-interaction testing as systems become more patient-facing, autonomous and consequential.
Finds synthetic data useful but warns synthetic patients are too tidy; wants messy behaviors modeled and generator bias considered, never replacing real behavior.
Wants re-testing scaled to whether a change could alter safety-critical behavior, treating such behavior as a protected function.
Wants regulators to define safety invariants, such as evidence grounding, escalation and human override, that cannot change without revalidation.
Sees master files improving efficiency but says voluntary transparency cannot replace required safety information or diffuse the device maker's accountability.
Defers on statistics but insists rigor cannot compensate for judging the wrong outcome, such as task completion instead of recognized urgency.
Urges FDA to focus on what a model does rather than what it is, keeping safety expectations constant across architectures.
Wants FDA to distinguish factual accuracy, task completion, clinical appropriateness, behavioral safety and patient outcome.
Wants testing of whether AI notices when a patient's literal ask differs from the need, especially in benefits, pharmacy, scheduling and cost interactions.
Wants safety-critical functions grounded in curated evidence with provenance rather than the statistical popularity of internet content.
Says professional licensure should not stand in for an evidence standard; AI should make departures from evidence visible rather than agree with clinicians.
Cautions that human in the loop says little; asks which human, with what qualifications, information, authority, time and real ability to override.
Wants surveillance to include litigation, state laws, board actions, enforcement and public reports, not only device adverse-event channels.
Calls for an interagency framework with coordinated jurisdiction over clinical-adjacent AI so no agency can say the problem belongs elsewhere.
Proposes fifteen patient-safety principles, from evidence grounding and restraint to auditability, accountability and regulatory continuity.
Proposes an influence-based principle: whoever deploys technology that foreseeably shapes care must prove it safe in proportion to that influence.
Closes on AI's potential to deliver the right knowledge where and when needed, reduce variation and help patients navigate a complex system.
Says correct answers cannot define success; healthcare AI should be judged on whether it helped the person get needed care, with escalation and accountability.
Urges FDA to work with federal and state partners on the territory just beyond the device boundary, since patients cannot tell the difference.
